summary.text: Electrical conductivity represents a material's ability to conduct electric current, and it is the reciprocal of electrical resistivity.
Resistivity measures how strongly a material resists electric current, so a low resistivity means the material readily allows current.
Unlike resistance, resistivity does not depend on shape, so all pure copper wires share one resistivity however long or thick they are.

facts.label: Usual symbols
facts.value: ρ for resistivity, σ for conductivity

facts.label: Rubber versus copper
facts.value: Rubber has a far larger resistivity than copper

facts.label: Resistance and shape
facts.value: Proportional to length, inversely to cross-sectional area

items.prompt: A lab sheet gives a material's resistivity, but you need its conductivity. What can you do?

options.label: Multiply it by the length of the sample
Square the value
Take the reciprocal of the resistivity value
Nothing, since the two are unrelated properties

items.explain: Conductivity and resistivity are reciprocals of each other, so each can be deduced from the other.

items.prompt: You apply the same electric field to a rubber rod and a copper rod. What happens?

options.label: Copper passes far more current, because it has low resistivity and high conductivity
Rubber passes far more current, because its resistivity is large
Both pass the same current, since the field is the same
Neither passes current, because a field alone cannot push charge

items.explain: Rubber has large resistivity and small conductivity, so even a very large field makes almost no current flow, while copper has small resistivity and large conductivity.

items.prompt: You swap a short, fat copper wire for a long, thin one made of the same pure copper. What changes?

options.label: Both its resistance and its resistivity go up
Its resistivity goes up, but its resistance stays the same
Neither changes, because it is the same metal
Its resistance goes up, but its resistivity stays the same

items.explain: Resistivity is intrinsic to the material, so pure copper wires of any shape share it, but a long, thin wire has a much larger resistance than a thick, short one.

items.prompt: In the pipe analogy for current, what does a pipe full of sand stand for?

options.label: A material with very high conductivity
A high-resistivity material that resists the flow
A short, wide piece of wire
A larger current flowing through

items.explain: Passing current through a high-resistivity material is like pushing water through a pipe full of sand, while a low-resistivity material is like an empty pipe.

items.prompt: Which quantity describes how a standard cube of material opposes current, whatever shape a particular object has?

options.label: Resistance of that object
Conductance of that object
Electric charge
Resistivity

items.explain: Resistivity and conductivity are intensive properties giving the opposition of a standard cube, while resistance and conductance describe a specific object.

items.prompt: A material resists current differently along different directions. Why can one number not describe its resistivity?

options.label: Resistivity then has directional components, so a fuller tensor form is needed
The material then has no resistivity at all
Resistivity can only be given for rubber
Directions change the unit from ohm-metres to siemens

items.explain: When resistivity has a directional component, the most general definition must be used; it is generalized to tensor quantities when the material is non-isotropic.
